abstract: The gut-brain pathways that transmit negative signals to the brain, influencing bodily functions and behavior, are not fully understood. We have identified a gut-brain axis in Drosophila that detects toxin-induced gut damage and triggers innate and learned, anticipatory emesis. Ingested toxins induce the midgut enterocytes to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS). ROS are detected by TrpA1 channels in enteroendocrine cells, resulting in the release of neuropeptides that signal gastric malaise. We also find evidence for midgut and ROS-independent mechanisms of toxin detection. Gut-derived neuropeptides act on brain serotonergic and dopaminergic neurons, which then communicate with the brain's sensory integration and memory centers, the mushroom bodies (MBs). This circuit enables vomiting and facilitates the formation of aversive memories. We find that the persistent activity of dopaminergic neurons mediates aversive reinforcement. Such activity lends itself to pairing the gut-derived malaise signal with odor representations in the MBs, enabling the flies to learn that the paired odor predicts toxin ingestion and to exhibit anticipatory emesis. Many components of this interoceptive pathway are likely conserved, providing a genetic model for exploring how aversive gut-brain communication influences metabolism, feeding, stress responses, and neurodegeneration.
